Request of Councilmember Zwick, Councilmember Raskin, and Mayor Pro Tem Torosis that the City Council direct the City Manager to return with options for revising development standards to effectively implement Housing Element Program 1.C.   CITY OF SANTA MONICA

  CITY COUNCIL MINUTES

  JULY 29, 2025

  A regular meeting of the Santa Monica City Council was called to order by Mayor Negrete at 5:34 p.m., on
  Tuesday, July 29, 2025, at City Council Chambers, 1685 Main Street, Santa Monica, CA.

  Roll Call:  Present:  Mayor Lana Negrete
  Mayor Pro Tem Caroline Torosis
  Councilmember Jesse Zwick
  Councilmember Dan Hall
  Councilmember Ellis Raskin
  Councilmember Barry Snell
  Councilmember Natalya Zernitskaya

  Also Present:  City Manager Oliver Chi
  City Attorney Douglas Sloan
  City Clerk Nikima S. Newsome

  CONVENE/PLEDGE  On order of the Mayor, the City Council convened at 5:34 p.m., with all
  members present. Councilmember Zernitskaya led the assemblage in the
  Pledge of Allegiance.

  STATEMENT OF  The City of Santa Monica is located on the land of Tovangaar. With
  ACCOUNTABILITY  great respect, the City acknowledges the Gabrieleño/Tongva as the First
  (LAND  People of this ancestral and unceded territory of Kuruvungna, a village
  ACKNOWLEDGEMENT)  that we know as Santa Monica. We honor their elders, past and present,
  and the Gabrieleño descendants who are part of the Gabrieleño /Tongva
  tribes.

  We recognize that these peoples are still here, and as settlers and kuyam
  (guests), we recognize our responsibility and obligation to care for their
  land in partnership with them. The City of Santa Monica commits to
  work in partnership with the Gabrieleño/Tongva people to uplift their
  voices and visibility on their ancestral land.

  The City of Santa Monica Statement of Accountability (Land
  Acknowledgement) was read into the record by Councilmember Raskin.

  these changes are leading to the construction of more units being built.

  Considerable discussion ensued on topics including, but not limited to the
  ordinance leading to the ability for older homes, often vacated after the death
  of elderly residents, to be transformed into multiple modest homes for new
  families, rather than being replaced by large mansions thus helping young
  families to be able to afford to live in Santa Monica; the history of single-
  family zoning as a tool for racial exclusion; similar ordinances in other cities
  (Portland, Berkeley, Houston, Austin, Minneapolis, Sacramento) that have
  led to increased affordability; affordability requirements for projects with
  more than five units to be able to include some affordable housing; concerns
  about increased density, scale, and the long-term livability of the community;
  upzoning could lead to more expensive, market-rate housing, displacement
  of lower-income residents, and strain on infrastructure; concerns about the
  use of emergency powers for non-emergency situations; the lack of
  meaningful affordability requirements, and the potential for gentrification
  and loss of neighborhood character; the need for anti-displacement measures,
  tenant protections, and ensuring that new development does not come at the
  expense of existing residents; and the need for more community engagement
  and a balanced approach that considers both housing needs and
  neighborhood impacts.

  Motion by Councilmember Zwick, seconded by Councilmember
  Zernitskaya, to adopt the staff recommendation. The motion was approved
  by the following vote:
